name: Kinshasa
subtitle: Kinshasa, capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo: its numbers, a short history and places to see beyond the World Heritage list.

keyPoints.text: About 7,273,947 people lived in the City-Province of Kinshasa in the 2004 official estimates (projected over 15 to 18 million today).
Kinshasa is the largest French-speaking city in the world and the third-largest metropolitan area on the African continent.
The 210-metre Tour de l'Échangeur and the new National Museum celebrate the monumental scale and artistic heritage of the Congo basin.

parts.text: Kinshasa was established in December 1881 as Léopoldville by Anglo-American explorer Henry Morton Stanley on the southern bank of the Pool Malebo, facing the Bateke settlement of Nshasa.
In 1923 it succeeded Boma as the colonial capital of the Belgian Congo, expanding rapidly into an industrial and river-port metropolis connected by railway to the Atlantic coast at Matadi.
Upon Congolese independence in June 1960, the capital became the vibrant political heart of the nation, officially rechristened Kinshasa in 1966 during the cultural campaign of Authenticité.

blocks.prompt: About how many people were estimated in the City-Province of Kinshasa in the 2004 official count?

parts.text: 7,273,947 in the 2004 official projections by the INS RDC. Modern demographic estimates suggest a megacity of 15 to 18 million residents, making it the most populous French-speaking urban agglomeration globally.

items.text: Henry Morton Stanley establishes the trading post of Léopoldville on the Pool Malebo.
Léopoldville replaces Boma as the colonial capital of the Belgian Congo.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo achieves independence.
The capital is officially renamed Kinshasa under the policy of Authenticité.
The 210-metre Tour de l'Échangeur in Limete is erected.
The state-of-the-art Musée National de la RDC opens in Lingwala.
